text: Vincent Price reads Robert Louis Stevenson over pictures of San Francisco, and the words and the images never quite agree. That gap is what Frank Stauffacher's twenty-two minutes are made of: a nineteenth-century poem laid across a working port photographed in 1951, hills and water and traffic moving to a rhythm the sentences were not written for. Nothing is explained. There are no interviews, no statistics, no case being argued; the film accumulates instead, one glimpse of weather or masonry after another, until the city registers less as a subject than as a set of surfaces the camera keeps going back to. Price holds his delivery low and level, which helps. The National Film Registry took it in, though the film asks for nothing so official — twenty-two minutes, and some tolerance for drift.

A widow with a small daughter and no income is, in Korea in 1955, less a person than a problem other people have views about. Park Nam-ok builds ninety minutes on that pressure. Lee Shin-ja needs money and also wants a life, and both roads run through her late husband's circle — his friend, that friend's wife, the wife's lover — so the same acquaintance who might cover her rent is the one who can undo her standing in a sentence. On paper the arrangement is close to farce; played straight, it is closer to a room with several doors and a watcher at each. The genre labels reach as far as thriller, which looks odd beside the domestic surface until the money is counted, at which point the suspense is plain enough. KOFA's hundred-title list is what has kept it in view.

The notice comes from a real estate agent rather than a landlord, and that detail carries the film. Lee Won-se gives this family everything but leverage: affection, routine, a father whose size makes him conspicuous on any street he walks down, and a house in the process of becoming a line in somebody's ledger. A hundred minutes, largely domestic, with a transaction for an antagonist — which means there is nobody to argue with and nowhere for the anger to land. The pressure sits in the distance between what the family is owed in fairness and what it can compel anyone to do. The film could easily have been shrill. It is patient instead, letting the ordinary business of a household run on right through the dispossession. KOFA's hundred includes it.

It started as a master's thesis, shot by a relief worker who was already in the country for other reasons. Twenty-nine minutes on Cambodia after Pol Pot, and the subject is not the killing but the work that follows it: a community trying to reassemble itself out of the people it still has. Ellen Bruno's position accounts for much of the film's temperature. She was not flown in for a fortnight, and the footage moves at the speed of the place rather than of a report. Mourning and reconstruction turn out to be the same labour, done by the same hands on the same afternoon. Films of this length about catastrophe usually argue. This one mostly attends. The National Film Registry has it, a peculiar fate for a student project and a deserved one.

A tramp watches a robbery happen and, instead of moving along, takes work on the farm nearby. Clarence G. Badger's fifty-five minutes from 1919 keep sliding between registers: comedy from a man who owns nothing and is in no hurry, Western from the country around him, drama from a villain with a grudge and Judge Hardy's farm to work it out on. What binds the mixture is the central figure's want of any stake — he is funny while nothing is required of him and becomes interesting the moment something is. The plotting is plain enough to follow a century on without help, and the farm supplies exactly the fixed address the man has spent his life avoiding. It sits on the National Film Registry, among pictures of far grander reputation, which is a decent joke on a hobo.

They meet only when it rains, which suits them, because both are lying. He repairs cars and lets it be understood that his father is in business; she works as a maid and is taken for the French ambassador's daughter. Chung Jin-woo does not puncture the deception early, so the film becomes a study in upkeep: two people managing clothes, addresses, vocabulary and the weather itself, since a clear day would demand explanations neither can afford. A hundred minutes in which little happens beyond maintenance, and the strain of maintaining does the work a plot usually does. It stays clear of cruelty because each is working exactly as hard as the other, and neither is a fool; what they lack is not wit but the money to make their stories true. KOFA's hundred keeps it.

The film was made to pay for passage home: fares for wounded Americans among the roughly 2,800 who enlisted in the International Brigades to fight for the Spanish Republic. That purpose governs all eighteen minutes of it. Henri Cartier-Bresson directed with Herbert Kline, and Jacques Lemare and Robert Capa supplied additional photography, which puts an unusual concentration of eyes behind what is, in form, a fundraising reel — people who knew how one frame persuades, working in a mode that must persuade before the collection is taken. It was shot in Spain in 1937, while the outcome was open and the argument still live. The print is held at New York University's Tamiment Library in the Abraham Lincoln Brigades Archive: an appeal made for one season, kept as a record of the men who answered it.

Flowers arrive at the theatre after every performance, with no card. Young-min saw Hye-rin once from the audience and has been sending them since, which is less a courtship than a practice, and Bae Chang-ho is interested in the practice. Nearly two hours go to duration rather than event: an attachment kept up across years, a marriage to a doctor, an address in New York, and a man not eloquent about any of it. The film risks airlessness and avoids it by keeping Young-min unremarkable in everything except persistence — no grand gesture is available to him, and the small ones are easy to miss. Waiting is the material here, held at a length that makes its cost legible rather than charming. KOFA's hundred lists it.

Colour film, in 1937, of a man in his garden. Cornelius Allen Alexander's twelve minutes at Tuskegee Institute in Alabama put George Washington Carver in four places he used daily — apartment, office, laboratory, garden — and nowhere else. It is not built as a portrait; it is nearer an inventory of rooms, and an inventory keeps what a portrait smooths away: the scale of a private apartment, the difference between a man at a bench and the same man among plants. Colour was uncommon enough in that decade for the choice to register as a choice, and it was spent on a working day rather than a ceremony. Twelve minutes is not long enough to explain anybody. It is long enough to have been in the room. The National Film Registry holds it.

The lecturer chain-smokes, and that is close to the whole of what she knows about him. Lee Myung-se stays inside the head of a first-year drama student who has fallen for a guest teacher old enough for the gap to be a problem, and who does with him what her training encourages: writes a part for him, and a part for herself opposite. A hundred and ten minutes given over to a feeling that keeps arriving ahead of any event to justify it. Comedy and discomfort come from one source — she is rehearsing a relationship that has not been cast — and the film declines to laugh at her, which is harder to manage at that age difference than it sounds. Interior weather is the entire subject, sustained for the full length rather than converted into incident. KOFA's hundred lists it.

The mountain last erupted around four thousand years ago and is still hot, which is a geological fact and, in this film, also a position in an argument. Puhipau and the crew of Na Maka o ka 'Aina spent five years on Mauna Kea, filming a summit at fourteen thousand feet and the ecosystems that step down from it to sea level. The patience shows in how the dispute is framed: not two spokesmen in chairs, but a place with seasons, stories and telescopes on it. What is at issue is jurisdiction — observatory site or cultural landscape — and the film takes its side plainly, treating the mountain as the most significant temple in the islands and reasoning outward from that. Fifty-seven minutes in which geology and legend are told in the same voice, and politics arrives as weather does.

While Seoul was preparing to be looked at by the world, the residents of Sanggye-dong were cleared out of the way of it. Kim Dong-won's twenty-seven minutes stay with them afterwards: the eviction first, then the slow, unphotogenic business of demanding somewhere else to live, which consists mostly of waiting on officials and refusing to disperse. The 1988 Games handed the government a deadline and handed the residents their only leverage, since nothing inconveniences a host city like a camera pointed at the district it would rather not show. The argument is not complicated: people had homes, and then did not. What gives the film weight is proximity — a camera still present after the eviction had stopped being news. It sits on the KOFA hundred.

Poverty here is not weather; it is a sequence of transactions, each with a man on the other side. Ida May Park's hour, made in 1918, follows a woman trying to climb out of it and finding every available route owned by somebody expecting payment in a form she never agreed to. The film is unsentimental about the arithmetic: work is scarce, the wage is small, and a favour turns into a debt without anyone naming the moment it changed. What keeps it from becoming a lecture is that it grants her intelligence — she reads the terms as clearly as the audience does, and usually sooner than the men assume. Sixty minutes, made at feature length inside the American industry of the day, by a director who evidently saw no reason to soften the account. The National Film Registry keeps it.
